items.content: Office of Science and Technology Policy News Our director Information & Resources Internships NSTC PCAST About Congress established the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) in 1976 to provide the President and Executive Office of the President (EOP) with advice on the scientific, engineering, and technological aspects of national policy and the work of the executive branch. This includes matters of the economy, national security, homeland security, health, foreign relations, the environment, education, and resource management. The OSTP Director oversees the development and execution of the nation’s science and technology policy agenda, leading White House efforts in critical and emerging technologies such as super intelligence, quantum information sciences, and biotechnology, with the aim of safeguarding US leadership in these fields and ensuring they advance in ways that bolster American economic competitiveness, national security, and human flourishing. The OSTP Director co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST), an advisory board whose members are drawn from outside the Federal Government, typically from industry, academia, and research institutions. The Director also chairs the National Science and Technology Council (NSTC), which coordinates the science and technology policymaking process across the executive branch to ensure delivery of the President’s agenda. In addition to leading interagency science and policy coordination, OSTP assists the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) with annual reviews and priority setting for the Federal research and development budget, and evaluates the scale, quality, and effectiveness of Federal science and technology efforts. OSTP also serves as a source of scientific and technical analysis and judgment for the President with respect to any major strategies, plans, and Government programs. CONTACT: To contact OSTP about stakeholder engagement, please reach out to us at: engagement@ostp.eop.gov To contact OSTP for press inquiries, please reach out to us at: press@ostp.eop.gov

items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports
items.content: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. items.title: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

items.content: Back to Articles How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications Team Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 33 +27 Bernardo França de Aguiar bernardoaguiar Follow Dharma-AI Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso GabrielPimenta99 Follow Dharma-AI Bruno Duarte brunoduarte01 Follow Dharma-AI Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves falves9101 Follow Dharma-AI Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications. In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model. The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step. One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency. The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses. We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication. A Vocabulary Built for Everyone The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense. For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once. The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request. The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses. Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill. To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill , the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode , the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth. This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading. Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings. The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model. And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows. Why Existing Solutions Fell Short Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations. They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve. They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one. How We Solved It VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first. First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly. Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget. To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points. Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain. An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated. A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running. That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%. What Changed in the Grader To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime. The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810. Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version. The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter. Beyond the Grader To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling. VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803. Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe. Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary. The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon. Sources Dharma-AI. "VocabX: Cost-Weighted Vocabulary Adaptation for Domain-Specific Language Models." In preparation (2026). Gee, Leonidas, et al. " Fast vocabulary transfer for language model compression ." EMNLP Industry Track (2022). Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Multi-word tokenization for sequence compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2023). Smith, Jimmy T.H., et al. " In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs ." arXiv:2607.15232 (2026). items.title: Make America Healthy Again
items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. Melania Trump Announces Halloween at the White House 2026 presidential actions FURTHER MODIFYING THE SCOPE OF PRODUCTS OF CANADA SUBJECT TO THE ADDITIONAL DUTIES IMPOSED TO OFFSET CANADIAN DISCRIMINATION AGAINST THE COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES WITH RESPECT TO MOTOR VEHICLES October 23, 2026 Read more : FURTHER MODIFYING THE SCOPE OF PRODUCTS OF CANADA SUBJECT TO THE ADDITIONAL DUTIES IMPOSED TO OFFSET CANADIAN DISCRIMINATION AGAINST THE COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES WITH RESPECT TO MOTOR VEHICLES promises made, promises kept 01 The Trump administration made incredible strides in its effort to Make America Healthy Again, with roughly 35% of the American food industry — including major corporations like Walmart, Hershey and Nestlé — agreeing to eliminate artificial dyes from their products. 02 At President Trump’s direction, the Department of Health and Human Services revised its childhood vaccine recommendations from 72 shots for 11 diseases to 10 “consensus vaccines.” 03 President Trump established the Make America Healthy Again Commission, tasked with investigating and addressing the root causes of America’s escalating health crisis, with an initial focus on childhood chronic diseases. 04 Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins signed a slew of waivers allowing states to remove junk food from SNAP. 05 The Department of Health and Human Services removed COVID-19 vaccines from the list of shots recommended for healthy children and pregnant women. 06 Following negotiations with the Trump Administration, a variety of major pharmaceutical companies have agreed to bring American drug prices in line with the lowest paid by other developed nations, ending decades of Big Pharma exploiting U.S. consumers. 07 President Trump secured $50 billion in funding for rural hospitals. 08 President Trump signed the Whole Milk for Health Kids Act into law, restoring nutritious whole and 2% milk in American schools. 09 The Trump Administration Rollins released new dietary guidelines that prioritize whole, nutrient-dense foods over processed junk. items.content: NVIDIA and Supply Chain Partners Expand Capacity to Accelerate AI Infrastructure Buildout New Capacity Agreements and Manufacturing Facilities to Support Volume Growth and Strengthen Supply Chain Resiliency October 21, 2026 News Summary: Substrate agreements with IBIDEN, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Unimicron Technology Corporation will, in aggregate, drive a 2.5x increase in capacity over the next three years. Amkor plans to increase its advanced packaging capacity by more than 300% by the end of 2028. KYEC will build new facilities in the U.S., supported by a $1.1 billion capacity reservation advance from NVIDIA. SPIL is targeting to increase its optical-engine capacity for co-packaged optics by 15x by mid-2027, with aims for another doubling by the end of 2028. GTC Berlin— NVIDIA today announced plans with a group of supply chain partners to expand global manufacturing capacity to meet growing demand for its accelerated computing and full-stack AI factory platform. Working with Amkor Technology , IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics , Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Unimicron Technology Corporation, NVIDIA is enabling new and existing suppliers to expand critical manufacturing capabilities across substrates, advanced packaging, testing and optical engines, strengthening the resiliency and redundancy of NVIDIA’s global supply chain. “We are in the midst of the largest infrastructure buildout in human history. Demand is extraordinary. Capacity is the constraint,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Our supply chain partners are the world’s best manufacturers. I’m grateful they are expanding capacity around the globe to scale production and help us deliver the AI supercomputing systems powering this new industrial revolution.” Expanding Substrate Capacity to Support Volume Growth NVIDIA plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5x over the next three years. The agreements below will contribute to this capacity expansion, with more underway. Under an agreement signed and announced earlier this year by IBIDEN, NVIDIA is providing a multibillion-dollar capacity reservation advance to support IBIDEN’s Ono Plant in Japan. The expansion targets capacity reaching 3x current levels at the plant, with additional capacity expected to begin ramping in the first quarter of 2028. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is joining NVIDIA’s substrate supply chain, bringing immediate capacity from its existing operations in South Korea. The collaboration also supports facility upgrades and new factories in Sejong and Busan, South Korea. By 2028, production allocated to NVIDIA is projected to account for a significant portion of Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ total annual package substrate production capacity. NVIDIA is supporting Unimicron’s KF substrate manufacturing expansion in Taiwan with a capacity reservation agreement. The expansion is expected to begin adding capacity in the second quarter of 2027 and reach full capacity by mid-2028. Scaling Advanced Packaging for Next-Generation Platforms NVIDIA and Amkor plan to expand advanced packaging capacity in South Korea, targeting a greater than 300% increase in interposer wafer capacity by the end of 2028. The planned capacity expansion, alongside Amkor’s development of new manufacturing facilities in South Korea, will support higher production volumes for NVIDIA’s current and next-generation platforms. Expanding Semiconductor Testing and Strengthening US Manufacturing NVIDIA expects its total semiconductor testing capacity to double from calendar 2026 to 2027, supported by buildouts in the U.S., Taiwan and Singapore. NVIDIA’s $1.1 billion capacity reservation advance to KYEC will support new U.S. testing facilities and equipment, with high-volume production targeted for April 2027. In Singapore, expanded testing operations are expected to begin high-volume production in February 2027. Creating the Infrastructure for Co-Packaged Optics NVIDIA and SPIL plan to expand manufacturing capacity in Taiwan for optical engines used in co-packaged optics, supporting the growing connectivity requirements of large-scale computing infrastructure. The expansion targets an increase of 15x by mid-2027, with aims for another doubling by the end of 2028. About NVIDIA NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is the world leader in AI and accelerated computing. items.content: Open source AI thrives when people come together to learn, build, share knowledge, and contribute. Behind every project is a community of developers, researchers, educators, and contributors helping make these technologies more accessible to others. The PyTorch Foundation Ambassador Program brings together community leaders from around the world who share that commitment. Through education, mentorship, technical content, community events, and open source contributions, ambassadors help expand awareness, adoption, and participation across the Foundation’s growing ecosystem of open source projects. The 2026 cohort welcomes 24 ambassadors across five program regions, representing communities from Nigeria and Burkina Faso to Singapore, India, Romania, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Each ambassador brings a unique perspective, technical background, and connection to their local community. Together, they are creating more opportunities for people to discover open source AI, develop practical skills, and contribute to the technologies shaping its future. A community shaped by many kinds of work The 2026 ambassadors bring experience across AI research, software and infrastructure engineering, technical education, open source maintenance, and community organizing. Some work on AI systems, model training, and infrastructure; others focus on documentation, workshops, mentoring, or applications that address challenges in their communities. Their work connects local communities with the PyTorch Foundation’s growing ecosystem of open source projects that help developers and researchers build, train, optimize, and deploy AI systems. Beyond the core PyTorch framework, this ecosystem includes projects such as vLLM, DeepSpeed, Ray, Helion, and Safetensors, spanning model training, inference, distributed computing, performance optimization, and model sharing. For someone new to PyTorch, that might mean attending a first hands-on workshop. For an experienced developer, it could mean discovering a new project, connecting with maintainers, or making a first open source contribution. An ambassador might help developers explore scalable inference with vLLM, introduce engineers to distributed AI technologies, or create technical content that makes complex concepts easier to understand. Meet the 2026 ambassadors The 2026 cohort brings together 24 community leaders across five program regions. AFRICA Adesina Lekan Samuel · Nigeria Soumana Dama · Burkina Faso Ronnie Atuhaire · Uganda Farah Abdou · Egypt Abraham Imani · Democratic Republic of Congo Simanga Comfort Mchunu · South Africa Mark Gatere · Kenya ASIA Alpha Romer Cooma · Philippines Tsai Li Ming · Singapore Mu Xiaohui · Singapore and Malaysia Wang Zhipeng · Singapore Sumantro Mukherjee · India Parichay Das · India Sudhir Dharanendraiah · India EUROPE Costin-Alexandru Deonise · Romania Ricardo Noriega · Spain Matthew Cossins · United Kingdom MIDDLE EAST Johnny Kozman · Egypt Ali Tavallaie · Armenia Amr Osama Abdellatif · Egypt Özge Çinko · Turkey NORTH AMERICA Aditya Mehra · United States Ali Gowani · United States Samaresh Kumar Singh · United States What being a PyTorch Foundation Ambassador means to our community For the 2026 cohort, being an ambassador is an opportunity to share knowledge, give back to the communities that shaped their journeys, and create pathways for others to learn and contribute. In their own words, ambassadors share what excites them most about joining the program. “Contributing to PyTorch documentation showed me how even a small contribution can become part of something much bigger. As a PyTorch Foundation Ambassador, I’m so excited to help more people experience that sense of belonging through practical learning, welcoming communities, and opportunities to contribute.” Özge Çinko · Turkey “Most of what I know about building AI I learned from open-source communities, so I’m excited to give back by teaching, mentoring and bringing more engineers from Egypt and Africa into the PyTorch ecosystem.” Farah Abdou · Egypt “As a PyTorch Foundation Ambassador, I’m excited to help more developers become open-source contributors through hands-on education and mentorship, while bringing the PyTorch and vLLM communities closer together in Singapore and across Asia-Pacific.” Mu Xiaohui · Singapore and Malaysia Together, these reflections capture what makes the Ambassador Program meaningful: a shared commitment to learning, collaboration, and helping more people participate in open source AI. Building the future of open source AI together Over the coming year, ambassadors will help create opportunities for developers, researchers, students, and open source enthusiasts to learn, connect, and contribute across the Foundation’s ecosystem. From introducing new audiences to PyTorch Foundation communities and related projects to supporting technical education and community collaboration, their efforts will help strengthen the global open source AI community. We’re grateful to this year’s ambassadors for bringing their time, expertise, enthusiasm, and generosity to the program. The strongest communities grow when people share what they’ve learned, welcome new contributors, and make room for others to build alongside them. We look forward to seeing what the 2026 PyTorch Foundation Ambassadors will teach, organize, create, and contribute in the year ahead. Learn more about the PyTorch Foundation Ambassador program at: https://pytorch.org/programs/ambassadors/

items.content: Featured projects When you’re speaking to a device, you expect text to appear as you talk. That makes streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR) a different challenge from batch transcription, where the model has the complete recording before it starts. Strong batch accuracy does not necessarily carry over into streaming. One cross-model ASR study illustrates this gap. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B achieved the best batch accuracy among the models tested, but its word error rate (WER) rose by 77% when evaluated with 2.4-second audio chunks. In that study’s cross-model streaming comparison (Table 5), NVIDIA® Nemotron™ Speech Streaming 0.6B had the lowest average streaming WER when operating over 560 ms audio chunks. The comparison makes a critical point: accuracy must be measured at the chunk cadence used in deployment. This case study takes the newer, multilingual Nemotron 3.5 from PyTorch to ExecuTorch and profiles its on-device execution on a Google Pixel 11. We ask how precision and chunk size change streaming quality, how much processing time the audio requires with one inference thread, where the workload spends its time, and which native kernels run. The goal is a practical way to evaluate accuracy and latency together. In this blog post, you will learn: How ExecuTorch connects PyTorch models to optimized Arm CPU kernels. Why streaming ASR needs its own quality evaluation, and how longer chunks improve final-transcript accuracy at the cost of higher latency. How Arm Scalable Matrix Extension 2 (SME2) reduces total ASR processing time with FP16 and INT8 quantization using per-channel weights (QC8W). How to combine model operator timings and native kernel samples to understand performance and identify remaining bottlenecks. How to choose chunk size and precision together to meet your accuracy and latency targets. From PyTorch model to CPU instructions ExecuTorch is PyTorch’s edge inference framework, with export tools and a lightweight runtime. The export process prepares the model for inference and produces a .pte file that the device runtime can load and execute. Supported operations are delegated to XNNPACK , a CPU inference library. On Android™, XNNPACK can select microkernels from Arm® KleidiAI™ software: small, optimized routines that perform the inner matrix calculations. Operators not delegated to XNNPACK run using ExecuTorch’s portable CPU kernels. Figure 1. From model export to CPU instructions. SME2 extends Arm’s instruction set to accelerate matrix calculations, including general matrix multiplication (GEMM). In the Arm C1 CPU cluster implementation with SME2, the matrix unit is shared by cores in the CPU cluster, and KleidiAI provides microkernels that use it for supported operations. Enabling SME2 in a build makes those paths available. However, native profiling is needed to show which kernels actually ran. What one streaming call contains Nemotron 3.5 is a multilingual streaming ASR model built around an RNN-T architecture with three parts: The encoder uses FastConformer attention and convolution layers to represent the audio. The predictor uses an LSTM to represent the history of emitted tokens. The joiner uses a small feedforward layer to combine the encoder’s audio representation with the predictor’s token-history representation and predict the next token. It can also produce a blank , which advances decoding to the next audio position. The frontend converts audio into log-mel feature vectors, producing one vector for every 10 ms . The encoder reduces the number of time positions by a factor of 8 , so its output has one position for every 80 ms of audio. This creates a more compact sequence representing the same audio duration. Figure 2. From waveform windows to streaming encoder positions. Lookahead is the future context available within a chunk; chunk cadence is how often fresh audio is collected for a call. At lookahead 13, a call collects 1,120 ms of audio and produces 14 encoder positions. The predictor and joiner processes all 14 valid positions , accumulating their tokens into the transcript. Lookaheads 0, 3, and 6 give 80, 320, and 560 ms chunks. Longer chunks increase the wait for the first text and subsequent updates; preprocessing and inference add time after audio collection. Choose chunk size and precision together We measured transcription accuracy on the host using the ExecuTorch runtime with its XNNPACK CPU backend. We created a local streaming adapter that uses the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard evaluation harness for dataset preparation, transcript normalization, and WER scoring. We evaluated FP32, FP16, and INT8 at four chunk sizes. The INT8 specification is QC8W which uses dynamic INT8 activations and per-channel INT8 weights for eligible linear operations, with FP32 outputs. Figure 3. Streaming WER versus chunk size across four corpora. Each point on the above figure covers 14,019 utterances from LibriSpeech Other (LS Other), AMI Cleaned, Earnings22, and VoxPopuli Cleaned AA datasets. WER divides total word errors by total reference words across all four corpora. Longer chunks improve final-transcript accuracy. From 80 to 1,120 ms, FP16 WER falls from 15.2% to 11.5% , and QC8W from 15.5% to 11.7% . FP16 essentially matches FP32 , differing by less than 0.03 percentage points at every chunk size, so we exclude FP32 from further performance analysis. QC8W preserves strong accuracy , adding 0.21–0.31 percentage points of WER relative to FP32. These host WER results inform precision and lookahead choices. However, it does not measure how long it takes for text to appear on the device. Test the real-time budget on an edge device We processed a 24.9-second recording on a Google Pixel 11 smartphone device using 1,120 ms chunks and one inference thread pinned to a mid-core CPU . We chose the mid-core CPU as a representative target for a sustained streaming workload on the system. We tested two builds of ExecuTorch 1.3.1, toggling SME2 support on and off. Each build retained XNNPACK and KleidiAI, and used identical model artifacts. Each configuration had two warm-ups and one measured tracing run. Totals cover processing the loaded recording from audio preprocessing through final detokenization. Figure 4. Whole-recording processing time with SME2 disabled and enabled. SME2 substantially reduces processing time: FP16 falls from 9.79 to 4.61 seconds ( 2.12x faster), and QC8W from 5.20 to 3.24 seconds ( 1.61x faster). With and without SME2, both process the recording in much less time than its audio duration. Dividing the processing time by the audio duration we calculate real-time factors of 0.19 for FP16 and 0.13 for QC8W (with SME2 on). This provides substantial processing headroom with only a single inference thread. Audio still has to arrive before it can be decoded, so this headroom does not remove the chunk-collection delay. But it leaves capacity for other CPU work between chunks and can help manage thermal load during sustained transcription. Find the bottleneck with ETDump ETDump records ExecuTorch operator events and timings. To understand where the 2.12X FP16 and 1.61X QC8W speedups come from, we grouped machine learning (ML) operators across the encoder, predictor, and joiner into categories: GEMM (blue): Matrix multiplication, mainly the encoder’s dense layers. Data movement (orange): Copies, concatenation, repeats, and embedding lookup. Elementwise (red): Activations, comparisons, and other per-value work. Convolution and normalization (green and purple): Convolution filters and normalization operators; both are relatively small here. Other (violet): Small remaining timed operations, such as tensor creation. Overhead (gray): Full-run time outside the grouped operator events; this can include runner and framework overhead. Figure 5. Operator costs and overhead behind the whole-run speedup. ETDump times are summed across the encoder, predictor, and joiner networks. Adding residual overhead gives the full processing time shown in Figure 4. GEMM drives most of the speedup. Enabling SME2 reduces GEMM time from 8.2 to 3.1 seconds for FP16 and 4.1 to 2.0 seconds for QC8W . GEMM remains the largest part of the run, though its share of total processing time falls from 84% to 67% for FP16 and 78% to 62% QC8W. Data movement takes roughly the same time for both builds, so its relative share grows as GEMM accelerates: from 8% to 17% for FP16 and 9% to 17% for QC8W. This remaining work limits the overall speedup and offers a target for further optimization. Which kernels ran? ETDump locates the expensive operator families, but does not name the native microkernels that execute them. Arm Streamline allows us to sample native call paths and measure hardware counters. On the Pixel 11, we measured 38.4% SME utilization for FP16 and 53.7% for QC8W . This indicates how much of each capture the matrix hardware was allocated; it is not a percentage of peak arithmetic throughput. We also sampled GEMM functions to identify the microkernels selected by each build. The function names reveal the sampled paths. The _sme2_mopa suffix denotes a matrix outer-product accumulation routine. NEON and I8MM are the vector instruction families used by the control paths. Precision SME2 Sampled GEMM paths and functions FP16 True KleidiAI FP16 SME2 kai_kernel_matmul_clamp_f16_f16p2vlx2_f16p2vlx2_2vlx2vl_sme2_mopa XNNPACK FP16 NEON xnn_f16_gemm_minmax_ukernel_6x16__asm_aarch64_neonfp16arith_cortex_a75 FP16 False XNNPACK FP16 NEON xnn_f16_gemm_minmax_ukernel_6x16__asm_aarch64_neonfp16arith_cortex_a75 QC8W True KleidiAI INT8 SME2, FP32 output kai_kernel_matmul_clamp_f32_qai8dxp1vlx4_qsi8cxp4vlx4_1vlx4vl_sme2_mopa KleidiAI FP32 SME2 kai_kernel_matmul_clamp_f32_f32p2vlx1_f32p2vlx1biasf32_sme2_mopa QC8W False KleidiAI INT8 NEON I8MM, FP32 output kai_run_matmul_clamp_f32_qai8dxp4x8_qsi8cxp4x8_16x4_neon_i8mm These captures confirm that SME2-targeted KleidiAI GEMM kernels ran on the Pixel 11 for both FP16 and QC8W, alongside other kernel paths. In the FP16 build, some GEMM operations still use NEON. In the QC8W build, some GEMM operations still run in FP32. This highlights a tooling gap in the ecosystem. ETDump exposes model operator timings, while Streamline samples native functions, but neither tool directly connects these views. Mapping individual model layers to the observed kernel functions remains future work. Choosing an operating point Deployment involves balancing response latency and accuracy across precision and chunk size. An application might start with an accuracy target or a latency budget; the following examples illustrate both approaches. Figure 6 below pairs the host WER results with a Pixel 11 component benchmark for SME2-enabled FP16 and QC8W. Grey ticks mark when audio collection finishes; dotted segments add the measured compute delay. The x-axis is a conditional time to first-token estimate : audio collection time plus the median encoder–predictor–joiner sequence time. The component benchmark used synthetic input, fresh stream state, and 75 measured samples per configuration across three rounds. It assumes the first output emits text. Figure 6. WER versus estimated first-token latency with SME2 enabled. For an illustrative 13% WER ceiling , both FP16 and QC8W qualify at 320, 560, and 1,120 ms chunk sizes. The 320 ms chunks favor earlier responses, with 12.67% WER for FP16 and 12.97% for QC8W . Longer chunks improve accuracy, reaching 11.50% and 11.72% , respectively, at 1,120 ms, but require more audio to arrive before transcripts begin to appear. For an 800 ms latency budget , both precisions at 320 ms and 560 ms fall within the budget and also below the illustrated 13% WER ceiling . The 320 ms configurations favor earlier responses while 560 ms gives better accuracy. At 560 ms, FP16 combines 12.01% WER with an estimated 691 ms delay, while QC8W combines 12.26% with 660 ms . Here, both 80 ms configurations miss the WER target. Conversely, both 1,120 ms configurations miss the latency budget. Conclusion: What does this mean for developers Evaluate streaming ASR at the intended chunk size. Whole-recording accuracy does not predict streaming quality. Longer chunks improve final-transcript accuracy here, while increasing response latency. ExecuTorch connects PyTorch models to optimized Arm CPU kernels. Its export and runtime path lets XNNPACK select KleidiAI microkernels for eligible operations. SME2 creates more processing headroom. Accelerating matrix work reduces the time spent on ASR, leaving more room for other application tasks or concurrent workloads on the device. ETDump reveals operator speedups and remaining bottlenecks. Grouping operator timings shows where the gains come from and how data movement becomes a larger share of processing time. Streamline identifies the native microkernels that ran. Native samples confirm selection of SME2 kernels, while hardware counters show matrix hardware allocation. Choose chunk size and precision together. Comparing precision and chunk-size combinations helps developers balance response latency against transcript accuracy for their application.

Convolution and normalization (green and purple): Convolution filters and normalization operators; both are relatively small here. Other (violet): Small remaining timed operations, such as tensor creation. Overhead (gray): Full-run time outside the grouped operator events; this can include runner and framework overhead. Figure 5. Operator costs and overhead behind the whole-run speedup. ETDump times are summed across the encoder, predictor, and joiner networks. Adding residual overhead gives the full processing time shown in Figure 4. GEMM drives most of the speedup. Enabling SME2 reduces GEMM time from 8.2 to 3.1 seconds for FP16 and 4.1 to 2.0 seconds for QC8W . GEMM remains the largest part of the run, though its share of total processing time falls from 84% to 67% for FP16 and 78% to 62% QC8W. Data movement takes roughly the same time for both builds, so its relative share grows as GEMM accelerates: from 8% to 17% for FP16 and 9% to 17% for QC8W. This remaining work limits the overall speedup and offers a target for further optimization. Which kernels ran? ETDump locates the expensive operator families, but does not name the native microkernels that execute them. Arm Streamline allows us to sample native call paths and measure hardware counters. On the Pixel 11, we measured 38.4% SME utilization for FP16 and 53.7% for QC8W . This indicates how much of each capture the matrix hardware was allocated; it is not a percentage of peak arithmetic throughput. We also sampled GEMM functions to identify the microkernels selected by each build. The function names reveal the sampled paths. The _sme2_mopa suffix denotes a matrix outer-product accumulation routine. NEON and I8MM are the vector instruction families used by the control paths. Precision SME2 Sampled GEMM paths and functions FP16 True KleidiAI FP16 SME2 kai_kernel_matmul_clamp_f16_f16p2vlx2_f16p2vlx2_2vlx2vl_sme2_mopa XNNPACK FP16 NEON xnn_f16_gemm_minmax_ukernel_6x16__asm_aarch64_neonfp16arith_cortex_a75 FP16 False XNNPACK FP16 NEON xnn_f16_gemm_minmax_ukernel_6x16__asm_aarch64_neonfp16arith_cortex_a75 QC8W True KleidiAI INT8 SME2, FP32 output kai_kernel_matmul_clamp_f32_qai8dxp1vlx4_qsi8cxp4vlx4_1vlx4vl_sme2_mopa KleidiAI FP32 SME2 kai_kernel_matmul_clamp_f32_f32p2vlx1_f32p2vlx1biasf32_sme2_mopa QC8W False KleidiAI INT8 NEON I8MM, FP32 output kai_run_matmul_clamp_f32_qai8dxp4x8_qsi8cxp4x8_16x4_neon_i8mm These captures confirm that SME2-targeted KleidiAI GEMM kernels ran on the Pixel 11 for both FP16 and QC8W, alongside other kernel paths. In the FP16 build, some GEMM operations still use NEON. In the QC8W build, some GEMM operations still run in FP32. This highlights a tooling gap in the ecosystem. ETDump exposes model operator timings, while Streamline samples native functions, but neither tool directly connects these views. Mapping individual model layers to the observed kernel functions remains future work. Choosing an operating point Deployment involves balancing response latency and accuracy across precision and chunk size. An application might start with an accuracy target or a latency budget; the following examples illustrate both approaches. Figure 6 below pairs the host WER results with a Pixel 11 component benchmark for SME2-enabled FP16 and QC8W. Grey ticks mark when audio collection finishes; dotted segments add the measured compute delay. The x-axis is a conditional time to first-token estimate : audio collection time plus the median encoder–predictor–joiner sequence time. The component benchmark used synthetic input, fresh stream state, and 75 measured samples per configuration across three rounds. It assumes the first output emits text. Figure 6. WER versus estimated first-token latency with SME2 enabled. For an illustrative 13% WER ceiling , both FP16 and QC8W qualify at 320, 560, and 1,120 ms chunk sizes. The 320 ms chunks favor earlier responses, with 12.67% WER for FP16 and 12.97% for QC8W . Longer chunks improve accuracy, reaching 11.50% and 11.72% , respectively, at 1,120 ms, but require more audio to arrive before transcripts begin to appear. For an 800 ms latency budget , both precisions at 320 ms and 560 ms fall within the budget and also below the illustrated 13% WER ceiling . The 320 ms configurations favor earlier responses while 560 ms gives better accuracy. At 560 ms, FP16 combines 12.01% WER with an estimated 691 ms delay, while QC8W combines 12.26% with 660 ms . Here, both 80 ms configurations miss the WER target. Conversely, both 1,120 ms configurations miss the latency budget. Conclusion: What does this mean for developers Evaluate streaming ASR at the intended chunk size. Whole-recording accuracy does not predict streaming quality. Longer chunks improve final-transcript accuracy here, while increasing response latency. ExecuTorch connects PyTorch models to optimized Arm CPU kernels. Its export and runtime path lets XNNPACK select KleidiAI microkernels for eligible operations. SME2 creates more processing headroom. Accelerating matrix work reduces the time spent on ASR, leaving more room for other application tasks or concurrent workloads on the device. ETDump reveals operator speedups and remaining bottlenecks. Grouping operator timings shows where the gains come from and how data movement becomes a larger share of processing time. Streamline identifies the native microkernels that ran. Native samples confirm selection of SME2 kernels, while hardware counters show matrix hardware allocation. Choose chunk size and precision together. Comparing precision and chunk-size combinations helps developers balance response latency against transcript accuracy for their application.

items.content: At a glance Harnessed Agentic RL: Microsoft Research Asia introduces a training paradigm in which the same agent harness used in deployment participates directly in reinforcement learning, removing the need to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. Lightweight by design: Agent Lightning v1.0 delivers a complete agent RL control plane in roughly 3,500 lines of code. Native Kubernetes support: agents run as standard Kubernetes jobs on self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure, with no dependency on paid commercial sandbox services. Data-efficient training recipe: an end-to-end coding agent pipeline raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, a 14.6 percentage point gain, using only about 6,000 training samples based on open sourced dataset. AI agents have evolved from single models to complex full-stack systems built from models, tools, and execution environments. Their capabilities increasingly depend on the agent harness that coordinates them from outside the model. Reinforcement learning (RL) is an approach where AI systems learn through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties for their actions. RL can make those agents better, but most agent RL systems require developers to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. That is costly, and it means the agent being trained is not quite the agent that gets deployed. To address this, researchers at Microsoft Research Asia have introduced the Harnessed Agentic RL training paradigm and open-sourced a fully rebuilt Agent Lightning v1.0 (opens in new tab) . Compared with the original, Agent Lightning, v1.0 puts more emphasis on staying lightweight, on integrating with real harnesses, and on a complete, reproducible agent RL training pipeline. Agent Lightning v1.0 was rebuilt around Harnessed Agentic RL, with key improvements: Lightweight : the entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code. Agent Lightning v1.0 implements a complete Harnessed Agentic RL system in a codebase that is small and clear enough to understand, modify, and extend. Training on a real agent harness : agents reach the model through the large language model (LLM) proxy in Agent Lightning v1.0, leaving existing harness code unchanged. Native Kubernetes support : agents run directly as Kubernetes jobs, without external commercial sandbox services. Self-managed clusters and local infrastructure alike can support rollouts at scale. A complete coding agent training example : an end-to-end pipeline built on Qwen3.5-9B raised Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8% to 56.4%, an absolute gain of 14.6 percentage points, using only about 6,000 training samples. The limits of traditional agentic RL Traditional agentic RL assumes the training framework owns the interaction loop with the environment. In a ReAct-style loop, the model generates an action, the environment returns an observation, the observation is appended to the context, and the model generates the next action, so the whole rollout maps onto one continuous token trajectory. Early RL systems such as verl, AReaL, and slime were built this way, which meant training an agent required rebuilding its loop inside the RL framework. Real harnesses have outgrown that assumption. Coding agents such as mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex each bring their own context management, tool protocols, execution logic, and dependencies, as do general-purpose agent systems. Rebuilding one for training is expensive, and the rebuilt agent may no longer behave in the same way as the deployed agent. Agent Lightning takes a different route. It places an LLM proxy between the agent and the model. The agent continues to run as before: simply point the endpoint that previously called the model API at Agent Lightning, and the training framework can observe and record its model calls. In v1.0, the researchers go further and formally define this paradigm as Harnessed Agentic RL: whichever agent harness is used in deployment is the harness that takes part directly in reinforcement learning during training (Figure 1). Figure 1. Traditional agentic RL compared with Harnessed Agentic RL. In traditional agentic RL, the training framework manages the environment and the agent loop. In Harnessed Agentic RL, the harness manages both. Four challenges in training with real harnesses A core difference between Harnessed Agentic RL and traditional agentic RL is that the environment interaction loop is handled by the agent harness rather than the training framework. The training system can only observe a series of LLM request and response pairs, so a single rollout may be split into a variable number of training samples. This brings four key challenges: Retokenization and sample merging : Harnesses keep context as text, but RL training needs the token IDs sampled during the rollout. Passing text through the chat template and tokenizer again can shift token boundaries, so adjacent calls cannot always be merged into one sample. Advantage calculation : Retokenization, subagents and context summarization can split one rollout into several samples. Computing baselines and advantages directly at the sample level causes rollouts that produce more samples to be counted repeatedly, which alters the original statistical relationships at the rollout level. Loss normalization : Averaging loss by sample count gives more weight to rollouts that produce more samples. Since sample count is often just a product of harness behavior, loss normalization must also avoid being distorted by it. Training backend scheduling : Sample count and length are known only after the harness finishes, while GPU counts and data/tensor parallel configurations are usually fixed. The backend has to map a variable workload into fixed resources. PODCAST SERIES Ideas Listen as members of the research community at Microsoft discuss the beliefs that animate their research, the experiences and thinkers that inform it, and the positive human impact it targets. Listen now Opens in a new tab Building a complete agent RL control plane in 3,500 lines of code In system design, Agent Lightning v1.0 treats simplicity as its first principle. The entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code, with three core components: the API Gateway, the Rollout Controller, and the Customized Trainer (Figure 2). The API gateway stores rollouts, models, and events, and serves as an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy. It links every model call from the harness to its rollout and records the prompts, responses, and log probabilities that training needs. The rollout controller starts and manages agent execution, either as local processes or as standard Kubernetes jobs, keeping agent execution separate from the trainer. The customized trainer, built on verl, creates rollouts, waits for them to finish, collects samples, and assembles the final training samples through a sample adapter. As a result, for an existing agent harness, simply pointing the model endpoint at the Agent Lightning proxy is usually enough to connect quickly to RL training. Figure 2. The Agent Lightning v1.0 system architecture showing the API gateway, rollout controller, and customized trainer. Collocated async RL Rollout times vary widely across agents. Synchronous RL waits for the slowest agent in a batch and leaves GPUs idle, while fully asynchronous RL raises utilization but needs separate GPU pools for rollout and training. In response, Agent Lightning v1.0 introduces Collocated Async RL, which lets rollout and model updates share the same set of GPUs. Once the system has collected enough rollouts, the update begins: the API Gateway pauses accepting new requests and waits for requests already in progress to finish, and rollout resumes after the update completes. The entire state transition is transparent to the external agent harness. In experiments, this approach achieved about a 2x end-to-end speedup over synchronous RL while using fewer GPUs than conventional asynchronous RL (Figure 3). Figure 3. Synchronous RL, asynchronous RL, and Collocated Async RL compared. Collocated Async RL raises utilization while occupying fewer GPUs. Running agents on Kubernetes Collecting enough rollouts means running many agents at once, which consumes substantial CPU, memory, and compute resources. Other Harnessed Agentic RL frameworks often host those agents on commercial sandbox services such as Modal Sandbox or E2B, where cost climbs quickly with scale. Instead, Agent Lightning v1.0 runs them as standard Kubernetes jobs, reusing existing self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure (Figure 4). Existing compute resources are used more efficiently, large rollouts cost less, and the whole pipeline stays open source and reproducible. Figure 4. The Rollout Controller in Agent Lightning v1.0 provides native Kubernetes support, running agents directly as standard Kubernetes jobs. 6,000 training samples, a 14.6-point performance gain To test the approach, researchers built a full pipeline on SWE-smith, mini-SWE-agent, and Qwen3.5-9B, covering data cleaning, environment construction, reward-hacking safeguards, and RL training. The training set holds about 6,000 samples and needs no large-scale compute. RL training alone raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified, a gain of 14.6 percentage points. The coding agent experiments further confirm the earlier analysis of two challenges: advantage calculation and loss normalization. Compared with sample-level handling, rollout-level advantage combined with rollout-level normalization achieves a higher validation reward and keeps policy entropy more stable during training (Figure 5). Figure 5. Pass rate and policy entropy for Qwen3.5-9B on the SWE-smith validation set. items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. PODCAST SERIES AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance. Listen now Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . items.raw_text: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions.
