Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241 , on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability. If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires. The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark. Results: the dependability column moved After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training. Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up. Model Retail Auto insurance Travel Neobank Consulting Overall Observed 20/20 Claude Opus 5.5 80.97 68.40 54.28 71.25 61.58 67.16 241 (47.53%) Claude Opus 5 80.71 65.80 49.95 70.62 66.19 66.50 241 (47.53%) GPT-5.4 76.33 62.65 68.12 65.34 54.60 65.36 128 (25.25%) GPT-5.6 Sol 67.65 65.30 60.34 59.09 57.52 61.91 82 (16.17%) Qwen3.8-27B RLFT 67.91 56.45 62.69 62.40 54.51 60.78 107 (21.10%) Claude Sonnet 4.6 72.35 54.40 58.94 56.39 54.31 59.19 102 (20.12%) GPT-6 Astra 71.73 46.55 55.87 60.87 56.83 58.31 231 (45.56%) Kimi-K3 82.24 50.80 61.83 41.35 51.63 57.37 68 (13.41%) Qwen3.8-27B 64.03 47.85 53.41 47.88 45.69 51.70 38 (7.50%) The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241. Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture. The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work . One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared. Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed. Where the gains landed Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric. Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points). What dependability costs The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time. Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20 Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage: Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts. Measure Base RL fine-tuned Change Campaign cost, 20 runs $925.80 → $855.58 −7.6% Cost per successful attempt $0.177 → $0.139 −21.4% Tasks passing 20/20 38 → 107 2.8× as many Cost per dependable task $24.36 → $8.00 −67.2% At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison. The single-attempt view Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1. Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier. The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range. The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset. These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most. The training loop Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench. Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run. Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat). Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py . For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps. Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures. That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool. Offline policy-relative difficulty Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer: No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation. ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim. Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] . If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] . In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another. ++ A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user. The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool? We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy. So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast. Estimating difficulty from limited probes Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability: success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½) Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards. We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass: Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper . One task, end to end Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update. Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band. When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1] . Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band. The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks. What earns a reward Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict. When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0. In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks. Two reward paths, one binary verdict Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed. Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test. Run the training stack We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training . The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are: docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting; docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration; docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20. Before you start Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv . You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency. The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark. Install Keep the three repositories side by side: mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1 git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0 Create the validated environment The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training uv venv --python 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606 python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install python scripts/verify_verl_install.py uv pip check The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel. Prepare the training data Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate python data/prepare_data.py -- help The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command. Configure and inspect the launch Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history. Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command: DRY_RUN= true ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run. Train The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray: # head node ROLE= head NODE_IP= " $HEAD_IP " GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh # each worker node ROLE=worker NODE_IP= " $WORKER_IP " \ HEAD_ADDRESS= " $HEAD_IP :6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node: export RAY_ADDRESS=auto export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \ trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md , then serve it with vLLM. From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration: vllm serve " $MERGED_MODEL " \ --served-model-name q38-rlft \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8001 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --language-model-only \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness: curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml ; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration: orchestrator: agent_model: type: aoai endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions deployment: q38-rlft credential: type: api-key api_key: <your_api_key> is_reasoning: true temperature: 1.0 top_k: 20 top_p: 0.95 max_completion_tokens: 8192 timeout: 1800 Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA . Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts: uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \ thinkingbox-eval \ --config " $PWD /thinkingbox.yaml" \ --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \ --dataset " $THINKINGBOX_DATA " \ --output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \ --errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \ --repeat 20 \ --coverage-profile full \ --aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \ --message-timeout 1800 The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation. Where this goes next The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards. If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records: Probe before you train. Take your own agent task set, run the base policy against it n times, and

items.content: Back to Articles Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 21 +15 Fearghal O'Donncha Fearghal Follow ibm-research Chandramouli Kamanchi rry003 Follow ibm-research Guruprasad Ranjini Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Natalia Martinez Gil natalialmg91 Follow ibm-research Bradley Eck bradleyjeck Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less guesswork about which model to use. Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task. Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed. The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast. Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from Hugging Face: pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11" import pandas as pd from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster df = pd.read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv" , parse_dates=[ "date" ], ) ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , ) result = ensemble( df.tail( 1024 ), timestamp_column= "date" , target_columns=[ "OT" ], context_length= 1024 , prediction_length= 24 , ) print (result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast print (result.quantile_outputs) # quantiles The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card . result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage. The ensemble members The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures: Model Architecture Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 Patched Transformer Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 Patched Conformer Granite FlowState-r1.1 State-space model Granite TTM-r3 Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer) For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper , PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview , FlowState paper , and Tiny Time Mixers paper . These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter. Two ways to combine the forecasts Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median. Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series. The forecast combination puzzle offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above. IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing. A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight. Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder: ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , subfolder= "recipes/granite-iqr" , ) Which method should I use? Your goal Start with Why A simple default Probabilistic Ensemble Equal influence, no fitted weights Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread IQR Ensemble Influence varies with each member's predicted spread Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon. Does the ensemble improve on its members? We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026. GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations. Lower is better. Forecast MASE ↓ MASE Rank ↓ CRPS / MWQL ↓ CRPS Rank ↓ Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob 0.683 ★ 47.175 ★ 0.471 50.948 Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR 0.684 48.773 0.471 47.619 ★ Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 0.685 51.371 0.467 ★ 48.918 Granite FlowState-r1.1 0.701 66.474 0.490 69.485 Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 0.717 74.794 0.488 68.134 Granite TTM-r3 0.724 83.062 0.520 88.959 ★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better. Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard. Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data. PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices. In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member. Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values. Extend the recipe to other forecasters The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve. The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them. For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing. Evaluate the recipe for your application GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data: Match your use case . Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve. Compare like with like . Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows. Look beyond point error . Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%. Measure the cost . Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload. Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment. Try it on your data The recommended starting point is the default four-model recipe: Granite Timeseries Ensemble on Hugging Face Getting-started notebook Granite TSFM repository GIFT-Eval benchmark Load the default recipe to get median and quantile forecasts from all four Granite architectures in one call, and adapt the recipe as your needs evolve. items.raw_text: Back to Articles Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 21 +15 Fearghal O'Donncha Fearghal Follow ibm-research Chandramouli Kamanchi rry003 Follow ibm-research Guruprasad Ranjini Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Natalia Martinez Gil natalialmg91 Follow ibm-research Bradley Eck bradleyjeck Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less guesswork about which model to use. Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task. Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed. The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast. Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from Hugging Face: pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11" import pandas as pd from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster df = pd.read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv" , parse_dates=[ "date" ], ) ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , ) result = ensemble( df.tail( 1024 ), timestamp_column= "date" , target_columns=[ "OT" ], context_length= 1024 , prediction_length= 24 , ) print (result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast print (result.quantile_outputs) # quantiles The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card . result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage. The ensemble members The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures: Model Architecture Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 Patched Transformer Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 Patched Conformer Granite FlowState-r1.1 State-space model Granite TTM-r3 Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer) For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper , PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview , FlowState paper , and Tiny Time Mixers paper . These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter. Two ways to combine the forecasts Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median. Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series. The forecast combination puzzle offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above. IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing. A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight. Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder: ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , subfolder= "recipes/granite-iqr" , ) Which method should I use? Your goal Start with Why A simple default Probabilistic Ensemble Equal influence, no fitted weights Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread IQR Ensemble Influence varies with each member's predicted spread Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon. Does the ensemble improve on its members? We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026. GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations. Lower is better. Forecast MASE ↓ MASE Rank ↓ CRPS / MWQL ↓ CRPS Rank ↓ Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob 0.683 ★ 47.175 ★ 0.471 50.948 Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR 0.684 48.773 0.471 47.619 ★ Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 0.685 51.371 0.467 ★ 48.918 Granite FlowState-r1.1 0.701 66.474 0.490 69.485 Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 0.717 74.794 0.488 68.134 Granite TTM-r3 0.724 83.062 0.520 88.959 ★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better. Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard. Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data. PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices. In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member. Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values. Extend the recipe to other forecasters The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve. The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them. For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing. Evaluate the recipe for your application GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data: Match your use case . Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve. Compare like with like . Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows. Look beyond point error . Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%. Measure the cost . Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload. Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment. Try it on your data The recommended starting point is the default four-model recipe: Granite Timeseries Ensemble on Hugging Face Getting-started notebook Granite TSFM repository GIFT-Eval benchmark Load the default recipe to get median and quantile forecasts from all four Granite architectures in one call, and adapt the recipe as your needs evolve. items.content: Back to Articles Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up Published October 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 24 +18 David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow In a previous post , we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do? The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself. Look up a model The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory. To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler ( neuronx-cc ) and of Transformers to look at. At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks. Run it yourself Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement : it loads the model with from_pretrained , sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron") . On a Trainium2 ( trn2 ) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container , install the packages, then run: python3 run.py No need for torchrun : the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded. A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version: hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache What "runs" means Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English. At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations. The results are a dataset Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions. Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet( "hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data" ) df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" ][[ "neuronx_cc" , "library" , "library_version" , "neuron_cores" , "result" ]] The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result. Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up . items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.32878 (cs) [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 26 Oct 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search Authors: Moritz Thoma , Maximilian Groezinger , Maximilian Forstenhäusler , Emad Aghajanzadeh , Manoj Rohit Vemparala , Christos Anagnostopoulos , Pierpaolo Mori , Nael Fasfous , Alexander Frickenstein , Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder , Ulf Schlichtmann View a PDF of the paper titled Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search, by Moritz Thoma and 10 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.7 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 19%. items.content: At a glance End-to-end forecasting: A machine learning pipeline uses forecast-time solar-wind information to generate location-specific risk estimates for 66,935 substations in the continental United States. Physics and place: The system combines Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) forecasts with local latitude, geology, and ground conductivity. Advance warning: The pipeline detected nearly 80% of major space-weather events during the evaluation period and can warn grid operators 30 to 60 minutes before a specific risk appears. Forecasting a threat to critical infrastructure During the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, utilities across North America prepared for possible impacts as auroras extended far beyond their usual range. The storm would degrade GPS accuracy and satellite operations, impacting farm operations in North America and Europe. Modern society depends on reliable electric power, yet extreme space-weather events can induce currents in transmission networks that damage equipment and increase operational risk. The challenge is not only knowing that a storm is approaching, but estimating when and where its effects could be most severe with enough warning for grid operators to respond. During my summer internship at Microsoft Research, I developed a machine learning system that forecasts space-weather risk across 66,935 substations in the continental United States. The system measures how the sun’s activity can affect the earth’s magnetic field and, ultimately, the power grid. It combines solar-wind observations, forecasts of the Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) indices, physics-informed constraints, local geological conductivity, and grid-infrastructure data to produce location-specific risk estimates 30-60 minutes ahead of potential impact. Building an end-to-end prediction pipeline Space-weather prediction is difficult because it spans several coupled systems. The solar wind changes rapidly, its interaction with Earth’s magnetosphere is irregular, and the resulting ground effects depend on local conditions. Regions with resistive bedrock can experience stronger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) than regions with more conductive geology. Transmission-line orientation, latitude, and other power-system characteristics further influence the exposure of individual assets. PODCAST SERIES AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance. Listen now Opens in a new tab The pipeline addresses this complexity in three stages, shown in Figure 1. First, solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point are used to generate forecasts of the AE and Dst indices, while geological conductivity and location features are assembled for each substation. Second, a gradient-boosting model combines these forecasted and location-specific inputs to estimate dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC risk. Finally, the resulting predictions are converted into location-specific risk estimates and aggregated into a continental risk assessment. A system of 50 AI agents helped explore features, validation strategies, and model configurations across the pipeline. Only public data sources were used, included NASA OMNI and NASA-aggregated Kyoto World Data Center data, INTERMAGNET and U.S. Geological Survey magnetometer observations, and GridSFM-derived grid data. Figure 1. End-to-end forecasting pipeline from L1 solar-wind measurements to location-specific risk estimates across 66,935 U.S. substations. Evaluating geomagnetic forecasts and infrastructure risk The AE predictor was designed to forecast rare, high-intensity geomagnetic activity that drives infrastructure risk. In the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the model produced forecasts spanning nearly the full observed range of AE activity and outperformed several empirical solar-wind-based approaches. The Dst predictor provided an additional signal describing large-scale geomagnetic storm strength. During the most geomagnetically active periods of the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the machine-learning model outperformed the Burton equation on 62.2% of individual hours. The model also produced a substantially wider prediction range than Burton-style approaches and improved severe-event detection in the end-to-end forecasting system by 1.2 percentage points when combined with AE forecasts. Predictor Result Baseline comparison Impact AE 410.2 nT RMSE Lower RMSE than empirical and solar-wind-only baselines Captures extreme-event activity used by the GIC forecasting system Dst 7.2 nT RMSE Outperformed Burton on 62.2% of peak-activity hours and provided wider prediction range +1.2pp severe storm detection when integrated into final GIC system The GIC risk stage was evaluated differently. There is no equivalent widely deployed operational system that provides a direct industry benchmark for this calculation, so the machine learning model was compared with simple linear regression. As Figure 2 shows, the system achieved detection rates of 76.5% for major events (≥10 nT/min), 81.2% for severe events (≥20 nT/min), and 64.1% for extreme events (≥50 nT/min). False-alarm rates increased with storm severity, reflecting the trade-off between missed events and cautious alerts. Performance varied by latitude, with the highest detection rates at northern stations where geomagnetic activity is strongest. Figure 2. Detection rates across storm-severity thresholds for regionally different substations, with a comparison between the average POD for each severity tier. Translating predictions into continental risk assessments The final stage translates predicted geomagnetic activity into location-specific estimates of dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC exposure. Rather than issuing a single alert for the continental United States, the system combines storm conditions with each substation’s latitude and geological factor. This produces continuous risk estimates that can distinguish lower-risk locations from areas where resistive geology can amplify ground-level effects. Figure 3 illustrates the output for a representative major-storm scenario. The map is a demonstration of the model’s continental-scale output, not a record of a live operational event. It shows how a grid operator or planner could move from a broad space-weather warning toward a more targeted view of which locations may warrant closer analysis. The current pipeline produced estimates for all 66,935 substations in approximately 333 milliseconds during measured inference, allowing many scenarios to be evaluated quickly. Figure 3. Demonstration of a continental GIC risk assessment under a representative major-storm scenario. Colors indicate modeled risk levels across 66,935 substations. Implications and looking forward This work demonstrates how physics-grounded machine learning could support more specific and timely assessment of space-weather exposure. Earlier, location-specific information could help utilities prioritize engineering review and consider targeted protective actions, such as adjusting reactive-power reserves or temporarily reconfiguring parts of the network. Further validation with utilities and operational data would be needed before the system could be used in grid operations. The project also connects with broader Microsoft Research work on AI for power systems. The open grid-data pipeline provided realistic U.S. transmission models, while GridSFM applies deep learning to AC optimal power flow for fast scenario analysis. Together, these efforts point toward richer planning and resilience workflows that combine hazard forecasts, grid topology, and power-flow analysis. Extend forecast horizons: Explore temporal-transformer approaches that capture longer-range patterns in solar-wind data and move beyond the current 30-60-minute window. Scale internationally: Adapt the system to additional regions while accounting for different geological conditions and grid topologies. Integrate with grid operations: Evaluate how forecasts could support existing decision-making and engineering-review workflows before considering higher levels of automation. Provide transformer-level risk: Add asset-specific characteristics to move from substation-level estimates toward more granular assessments of critical equipment. Related Microsoft Research work Video playback requires cookie consent GridSFM: A new, small foundation model for the electric grid Building realistic electric transmission grid dataset at scale: a pipeline from open dataset Acknowledgements Special thanks to my mentors Weiwei Yang and Spencer Fowers for their guidance throughout this project, and to Amber Hoak , Weishung Liu , and Andrea Britto for their editorial and technical feedback. The architecture aligns with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and defines coordinated requirements across compute, networking, storage, power, liquid cooling, cabling, and mechanical design. Factory integration moves complex assembly and testing into a controlled environment while site teams prepare foundations, power, and external connectivity in parallel. Standardized container interfaces enable repeatable capacity expansion and a consistent foundation for software optimization across deployments. NVIDIA provides the validated design foundation while ecosystem partners handle manufacturing, regional engineering, customization, deployment, and support. Next Steps Learn more about the NVIDIA DSX POD reference design to evaluate how it can accelerate AI factory deployment. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more AI factories turn energy into intelligence. But before an AI workload can produce its first token, operators must bring an interconnected system of compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, and software online as one productive unit. In a conventional data center build, teams must first select the site, design power and cooling for the deployment, lay out the data center, and plan and install racks and cables. Then they can validate the network and cluster incrementally and bring service online. This work requires coordinated specialized labor, with critical dependencies among installation, infrastructure readiness, and system testing. Delays can push back bring-up and the date the infrastructure begins producing tokens. NVIDIA DSX POD shifts more of this work into a controlled factory environment. One of multiple AI factory implementation models supported by NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is the standardized, factory-built implementation. It enables partners to build standardized containers that pre-integrate AI infrastructure, complete critical validation before shipment, and connect to prepared site infrastructure after delivery. The result is a repeatable approach designed to reduce onsite integration complexity and help operators reach productive AI capacity faster and more predictably. This post explains the foundation of NVIDIA DSX POD, how the reference design aligns with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform , and how NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners work through product engineering, deployment, and support. A design foundation for moving AI factory integration upstream Modular and prefabricated data centers already exist. The engineering challenge for an AI factory extends beyond placing conventional IT equipment in an enclosure. Rack-scale AI systems combine high-density compute, high-speed scale-up and scale-out networking, liquid cooling, power delivery, telemetry, and management software. These elements behave as one system. Their mechanical, electrical, thermal, and network requirements must remain within specification during factory integration, transportation, installation, and operation. NVIDIA DSX POD provides the design foundation for partners to install rack-scale systems in containers at the factory, functionally test the integrated unit, transport it, and bring it online safely through repeatable processes at the destination. NVIDIA’s investment spans the engineering disciplines required to make that possible, including rack layout, structural loading, power, cooling, cabling, service access, reliability, and validation. This work extends the progression toward greater factory integration to reduce installation complexity and accelerate deployment. NVIDIA has moved from chips and boards to complete rack-scale systems, and large-scale reference architectures like NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD . NVIDIA DSX POD carries this approach into a factory-built AI factory implementation, moving most component integration from the customer site into a controlled manufacturing environment. The reference design does not make containerization mandatory for every AI factory. Conventional data center construction and onsite-integrated designs remain important options. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: October 26, 2026 Back to Top
